prize_parts.citation: For developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets from market data, which made it possible to measure substitution, market power and welfare effects credibly.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is still B005 with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. My configuration changed in one respect, the citation. In round 1 I wrote dynamic industry models into the wording. After the exchange I think that was a mistake. The dynamic strand is Pakes's, with Benkard, Levin and others, and Berry and Levinsohn are not credited for it. A three-name citation that includes it overstates what the trio shares and invites the Benkard-Levin objection. I therefore anchor the citation on the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand-estimation core and mention Pakes's dynamic work only as supporting depth, not as part of the prize text. The names and the ballot are unchanged. The chair asks for one test applied to all four leading candidates, so here is mine: (1) did the work change what can be credibly known, (2) has that been validated in use or in evidence over a long period, (3) is the credit identifiable within three names, and (4) is the contribution distinct from earlier prizes? B005 satisfies all four on the evidence in the files. It makes price elasticities, market power and merger effects estimable from market data, and it has about three decades of use, with no prior-prize overlap raised by any member. B014 does well on maturity and coherence, but its cross-country identification is weaker and the 2024 overlap has to be argued. B027 is conceptually original and cleanly credited, but its validation is indirect and the 2022 prize is adjacent. B030 has strong design-based evidence, but the magnitude and persistence debate and the Dorn-versus-Katz and task-framework credit questions are still open. This is a weighing on common criteria, not a count. Five of eleven first choices says nothing about merit, and I have not verified any of the factual claims in the round-1 files.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged: this is a methods and measurement prize, and the Committee may weigh it below a candidate that answers a first-order substantive question. I have given an argument that measurement can itself be the discovery, but I cannot show that the Committee should accept it. The three-name cap forces an exclusion. Bresnahan and Reiss, who founded the earlier new empirical IO tradition, and Benkard and Levin, on dynamic estimation, all have real claims. Narrowing the citation reduces the attribution problem but does not remove it. Structural estimates also depend on functional form, instruments and equilibrium assumptions, so the credibility of individual applications varies. I also cannot independently check the claims about breadth of use that carry much of my case.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) ranks B014 first. He says the Persson-Tabellini-Besley programme is distinct from the 2024 institutions prize because it concerns policy choice under given rules, and he says he would move to B005 if the overlap were judged decisive.
responses.response: I accept the distinction he draws, and since I gave the 2024 presentation speech I see the line between long-run institutional origins and policy choice under given electoral and constitutional rules clearly enough. I do not think overlap is a bar. My difference with him is about identification. The 2024 award rested on a design that supports a causal reading, and the speech made that a central point. The cross-country evidence for constitutional and electoral-rule effects supports weaker claims, and the within-country and state-capacity strands he cites are narrower. If the Committee recognises B014, I would want a citation that does not overclaim causal findings. I note his stated conditional movement toward B005 but do not rely on it, and I am not asking him to change his preferred part.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B027 first. He weights conceptual originality and durable influence on how macroeconomists think above the number of fields that use a tool. He concedes that the amplification mechanism is validated mostly indirectly and that the 2022 prize is adjacent.
responses.response: His own concession is where we separate. I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-person attribution, and I would not add Gertler or Gilchrist. On originality I think the two candidates are close. Both introduced a mechanism or measurement approach that was not available before, and the Committee could reasonably say that B027 is the more novel idea. The validation difference is the reason I rank B005 higher. The BLP toolkit has been tested directly by thousands of applications and by regulators, while the collateral-constraint mechanism has been supported mostly by later work of others. I would not dismiss his criterion, and B027 remains my second alternative. If the Committee puts conceptual originality ahead of validation, B027 moves ahead of my current ordering.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B005 last in his opening because of diffuse attribution and sensitivity to implementation. In round 1 he says he was moved by the breadth-of-use argument and now lists B005 as his first alternative. He still prefers B027 and defers to IO specialists on Levinsohn versus Bresnahan.
responses.response: His revision is useful, and I do not read it as support for B005 over B027, since he states his preference clearly. His remaining concern about implementation sensitivity is real, and I have it in my case against. I read it as a limit on how applications are judged, not as a flaw in the originality of the method. On his deferral on the third name, I should say that I am not an IO specialist either. My argument for Levinsohn rests on the structure of the citation, not on expertise, and I would accept Bresnahan only if the citation were widened to the earlier inference-of-market-power tradition. His point that breadth of use should be applied equally to Kiyotaki-Moore is fair, and my test above is meant to apply to every candidate.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 first and lists B005 as his main alternative. He names a Persson-Tabellini two-person core as a fallback, says Besley's state-capacity strand is the part most exposed to the 2024 overlap objection, and wants the citation worded to avoid causal overclaiming.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point, and it is where my reservation about B014 is sharpest. A citation framed around theory plus evidence on how electoral rules and constitutions shape fiscal policy is defensible. One that implied settled causal effects would not be. His fallback to a Persson-Tabellini core is a coherent choice, and I would find it easier to support than a three-name B014 that includes the strand closest to the 2024 agenda. I do not take his stated willingness to support B005 over weaker options as agreement on merit. I take it as a candid statement of how he weighs the two. B014 remains my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats a measurement and estimation contribution as meeting the bar against candidates with a clearer substantive headline result, when no agreed test exists. My test favours B005, and I recognise that a member with a different weighting could apply the same four criteria and reach a different order.

Whether the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core should be credited alone or whether the broader empirical-IO tradition (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard, Levin) should be recognised. That would need a different citation and credit set, and I would reconsider if colleagues argue that the earlier tradition is the more faithful account of how the field developed.

How much of the B014 evidence on electoral rules and constitutions supports a causal claim strong enough for a citation, and whether the 2024 prize makes the Committee reluctant to recognise institutions-related work this soon.
Whether indirect validation of the B027 mechanism should count against it for a contribution of this age. This could reorder my alternatives.
I have not independently verified any claims about prior prizes, citation counts, replication records or the dates of contributions. My assessments rest on the files and on my own judgement.
statement.conflict_note: Updated in answer to the chair's question. In round 1 I wrote that my profile names no personal, collaborative or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley, and I stand by that as to the supplied profile's explicit collaborator lists. The profile does mention a Governance paper on corruption as a collective-action problem written 'with Persson and Rothstein', without giving a first name. I cannot establish from the supplied evidence which Persson that is, and I will not assume. I disclose it so that Hassler's reference is not left unreconciled, without claiming that it is or is not Torsten Persson. I also share Stockholm University with IIES committee colleagues, in a different department, and I cannot confirm from the profile whether any B014 name is affiliated there. B014 is only an alternative for me, and my field (democratisation and institutions) and my 2024 presentation speech are close to its topic. For B005 and B027 I have no apparent tie to any credited name. These are disclosures, not adjudications.
